metadata.name: Haemorrhoids (piles)
metadata.emergency_level: Routine - but do NOT attribute rectal bleeding to piles without excluding cancer; thrombosed pile is acutely painful
metadata.severity: Usually mild; bleeding, prolapse and pain can affect quality of life

overview.short_description: Enlarged, symptomatic anal vascular cushions causing bright-red rectal bleeding on defecation, itching, prolapse or discomfort; usually managed conservatively.
overview.detailed_description: Haemorrhoids are very common and usually benign. The cardinal caution is that rectal bleeding must not be assumed to be from piles until colorectal cancer has been considered/excluded, especially with red flags or in older patients. Internal haemorrhoids are graded I-IV; treatment is stepwise from lifestyle/topical measures to outpatient procedures (banding) and surgery. Thrombosed external haemorrhoids cause acute severe pain.
overview.pathophysiology: Increased pressure/straining and connective-tissue laxity engorge and prolapse the anal vascular cushions; internal (above dentate line, painless bleeding) and external (below, can thrombose and be painful).
overview.etiology: Chronic straining/constipation, low-fibre diet, prolonged sitting, pregnancy, ageing, raised intra-abdominal pressure.
overview.natural_history: Often intermittent and chronic; may improve with bowel-habit correction or progress/prolapse.
overview.prognosis: Good; the key risk is a missed colorectal cancer if bleeding is not properly assessed.

prevalence.value: Very common; a large proportion of adults are affected at some time.

incidence.value: High; peaks in middle age and pregnancy.

epidemiology.age_groups: Adults; common in pregnancy and with age.

risk_factors.lifestyle: Low-fibre diet, straining, prolonged sitting/toilet time, heavy lifting.
risk_factors.family_history: Colorectal cancer history (red flag for bleeding assessment).
risk_factors.previous_diseases: Chronic constipation; portal hypertension (anorectal varices - a mimic).

chief_complaints.importance: Classic symptom - but must exclude cancer

symptoms.symptom: Bright-red painless bleeding, coating stool or on paper
symptoms.importance: Cardinal symptom of internal haemorrhoids (colour/pattern; still exclude cancer)

symptoms.symptom: Prolapsing anal lump (reduces spontaneously or manually)
Acute severe anal pain with a tender lump (thrombosed external haemorrhoid)
Change in bowel habit, weight loss, dark blood/mixed in stool (RED FLAGS)
symptoms.importance: RED FLAGS - not typical of piles; investigate for cancer

negative_findings.finding: Bleeding is bright red, on the surface/paper, without change in bowel habit, weight loss or anaemia
negative_findings.why_important: More consistent with haemorrhoids - but does NOT exclude cancer; assess by age/risk

negative_findings.finding: Normal examination apart from haemorrhoids; no mass on rectal exam
negative_findings.why_important: Supports benign cause (but proximal lesions need endoscopy where indicated)

history_questions.question: Is the blood bright red on the surface/paper, and is there a lump?
Any change in bowel habit, weight loss, dark or mixed-in blood, or anaemia symptoms?
How old are you and any family history of bowel cancer?
Any severe acute anal pain (thrombosis) or signs of anaemia?
history_questions.why_ask: Acute painful pile / significant blood loss

physical_examination.examination: Inspection of the anus (prolapse, external/thrombosed haemorrhoids, skin tags, fissure)
physical_examination.expected_finding: Visible haemorrhoids/prolapse; thrombosed pile is a tender purple lump
Assess for a mass (internal haemorrhoids are often not palpable); exclude rectal tumour

laboratory_tests.expected_result: May show iron-deficiency anaemia (anaemia is a red flag - not to be attributed to piles alone)

laboratory_tests.indication: Red flags, older age, or diagnostic uncertainty about the bleeding source

imaging.when_needed: Colonoscopy/flexible sigmoidoscopy if proximal source needs exclusion

other_diagnostic_tests.endoscopy: Proctoscopy to confirm/grade haemorrhoids; colonoscopy if red flags/older to exclude proximal disease

diagnostic_criteria.formal_criteria: Clinical diagnosis on history and examination (inspection, digital rectal exam, proctoscopy). Internal haemorrhoids graded I (bleed, no prolapse) to IV (irreducible prolapse). Crucially, rectal bleeding is only attributed to haemorrhoids AFTER excluding colorectal cancer per age/risk and red flags.

differential_diagnosis.differences: Change in bowel habit, weight loss, anaemia, dark/mixed blood, older age
differential_diagnosis.red_flags: Weight loss, altered bowel habit, anaemia
differential_diagnosis.differential_questions: Any change in bowel habit, weight loss, or blood mixed in the stool?

differential_diagnosis.differences: Severe pain ON defecation, small tear seen posteriorly
differential_diagnosis.differential_questions: Is there sharp pain on passing stool?
Any diarrhoea, urgency, or mucus with the bleeding?

diagnostic_questions.question: Any change in bowel habit, weight loss, anaemia, or dark/mixed-in blood?
diagnostic_questions.purpose: Ensure bleeding is not from cancer
diagnostic_questions.interpretation: Red flags -> investigate/refer; do not attribute to piles

diagnostic_questions.question: Is the pain acute and severe with a tender lump (thrombosis)?
diagnostic_questions.interpretation: Positive -> analgesia; consider excision if within ~72h and severe

next_best_question.question: Any red flags, your age/family history, and examination findings (mass on rectal exam)?
next_best_question.branching_logic: Red flags/older -> colorectal investigation; benign -> conservative haemorrhoid management + bowel-habit correction; large/refractory -> banding/surgery

next_best_test.why: Confirm/grade haemorrhoids and exclude a low rectal mass

red_flags.finding: Rectal bleeding with change in bowel habit, weight loss, anaemia, or dark/mixed-in blood
red_flags.immediate_action: Urgent colorectal investigation - do not attribute to haemorrhoids

red_flags.finding: Abdominal or rectal mass on examination

referral_criteria.urgent_referral: Red-flag rectal bleeding (cancer pathway); strangulated haemorrhoids.
referral_criteria.routine_referral: Symptomatic haemorrhoids not responding to conservative measures (for banding/surgery).

initial_management.supportive_care: Explain and reassure after excluding serious causes; correct constipation/straining.
initial_management.medications: Canonical schema 1.3 guidance: use treatment_guidance.medication_options and its history-based safety checks. Candidate classes/options (not a prescription): Fibre and stool-softening regimen; Short-course topical anorectal preparation. No autonomous selection or dosing is allowed. Source IDs: ASCRS_HEM_2024.
initial_management.lifestyle_advice: Increase fibre/fluids, avoid straining and prolonged toilet sitting, good anal hygiene.
initial_management.follow_up: Review response; refer for procedures if persistent; ensure red-flag bleeding is investigated.
initial_management.legacy_medications_pre_v13: High-fibre diet and fluids; bulk-forming laxatives to avoid straining; topical preparations (soothing +/- short-term local anaesthetic/steroid) for symptom relief; simple analgesia and topical measures for thrombosed piles. Outpatient procedures (rubber-band ligation) or surgery (haemorrhoidectomy) for higher-grade/refractory disease.

patient_education.home_advice: Piles are swollen blood vessels around the back passage that can cause bright-red bleeding, itching or a lump. They are common and usually settle with more fibre and fluids to keep stools soft, avoiding straining, and soothing creams. Importantly, never assume bleeding is 'just piles' - see a doctor to be checked, especially if you have a change in bowel habit, weight loss, or the blood is dark or mixed into the stool.
patient_education.home_advice_ar: البواسير أوعية دموية منتفخة حول فتحة الشرج قد تسبّب نزفاً أحمر فاتحاً أو حكّة أو كتلة. وهي شائعة وتتحسّن عادةً بزيادة الألياف والسوائل لتليين البراز، وتجنّب الحزق، والمراهم المهدّئة. والمهم: لا تفترض أن النزف «مجرّد بواسير» - راجع الطبيب للفحص، خاصةً إن تغيّرت عادة الأمعاء، أو نقص وزنك، أو كان الدم غامقاً أو مختلطاً بالبراز.
patient_education.prevention: Fibre, fluids, avoid straining and prolonged sitting on the toilet.
patient_education.warning_signs: Change in bowel habit, weight loss, dark/mixed-in blood, heavy bleeding, or a painful irreducible lump.

evidence.evidence_level: Moderate-high for fibre and procedural treatments.
evidence.guideline_strength: The main diagnosis/test and treatment direction was checked against the current guidance identified by ASCRS_HEM_2024; see evidence_review for scope and limitations. This does not verify every legacy narrative sentence.
evidence.legacy_guideline_strength_pre_v13: Strong - NICE CKS, ASCRS/colorectal society guidance.

treatment_guidance.legacy_narrative_summary: Canonical schema 1.3 guidance: use treatment_guidance.medication_options and its history-based safety checks. Candidate classes/options (not a prescription): Fibre and stool-softening regimen; Short-course topical anorectal preparation. No autonomous selection or dosing is allowed. use_caution_if: faecal impaction, severe dehydration, CKD for magnesium/phosphate products, electrolyte disturbance, or swallowing difficulty for bulk fibre
monitoring: stool response, hydration and electrolytes when risk/product warrants
